title: AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Strix Halo): 16 Zen 5 Cores, 40 CU RDNA 3.5 & 256-bit Unified Memory vs. RTX 4070 Mobile & Apple M4 Max (2026 Breakdown)
excerpt: AMD Strix Halo revealed: Ryzen AI Max+ 395 packs 16 Zen 5 cores, 40 CU RDNA 3.5 graphics, and 256-bit unified memory to challenge Apple M4 Max and RTX...
content:
The Monolithic Paradigm Shift: AMD Direct Challenge to Unified Memory Monopolies

For more than a decade, x86 laptop architectures maintained a rigid structural divide: lightweight integrated graphics for daily display output and power-hungry discrete graphics cards connected via discrete PCIe lanes for demanding rendering, compute, and gaming tasks. While this dual-silicon approach delivered high peak rasterization performance, it introduced severe thermal compromises, motherboard layout complexities, high manufacturing costs, and rigid video RAM boundaries. When an artificial intelligence model or open-world gaming asset cache exceeds physical mobile VRAM allocations—typically capped at 8GB on midrange Nvidia mobile chips or 16GB on high-end laptops—performance plummets as assets crawl across the system bus.

AMD has shattered this limitation with the official architecture launch of Strix Halo, commercially designated as the Ryzen AI Max+ 395. Designed from the ground up to challenge Apple M-series unified memory architecture on high-performance x86 hardware, this processor fuses 16 high-performance Zen 5 CPU cores (32 execution threads) with a massive 40 Compute Unit (CU) RDNA 3.5 graphics engine on a single unified socket package. Backed by a wide 256-bit LPDDR5X-8533 memory interface, Strix Halo delivers up to 273.0 GB/s of sustained memory throughput, providing both the processor and the graphics cluster direct access to up to 128GB of high-speed system memory.

Silicon Floorplan: Dual Zen 5 CCDs and the Massive Central Graphics Die

Unlike traditional monolithic mobile processors that compromise either CPU core counts or GPU shader arrays to manage die sizes, the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 employs an advanced multi-die chiplet topology manufactured on TSMC advanced 4nm (N4P) process node:

  • Dual 8-Core Zen 5 CCDs: The processor incorporates two complete Core Complex Dies (CCDs), each featuring 8 full-power Zen 5 cores with dedicated 32MB L3 caches per complex (64MB total L3 cache). Unlike dense compact Zen 5c cores, every core on the Max+ 395 sustains full boost clocks up to 5.1 GHz with expansive instruction pipelines.
  • The 40 CU RDNA 3.5 Graphics Engine: Occupying the bulk of the main system die is an enormous integrated GPU featuring 2,560 stream processors, 80 AI Matrix Accelerators, and 40 Ray Accelerators. Operating at GPU clock frequencies up to 2.9 GHz, this engine delivers 29.7 TFLOPs of peak single-precision compute horsepower—matching the raw shader count of a desktop Radeon RX 7600 XT or an RTX 4070 mobile chip.
  • 32MB Dedicated MALL Cache: To alleviate memory bus saturation during intense 3D texture filtering and frame generation, AMD integrated 32MB of Memory-Attached Last-Level (MALL) cache directly onto the GPU subsystem, acting as a high-speed buffer similar to desktop Infinity Cache.
  • 50 TOPS XDNA 2 Neural Processing Unit: Compliant with Microsoft Copilot+ requirements, the onboard NPU executes local FP16 and block-quantized INT8 matrix operations independently, handling background telemetry, computer vision, and real-time audio isolation with minimal battery draw.

Technical Architecture Matrix: Ryzen AI Max+ 395 vs. Competitors

To evaluate how AMD flagship APU stacks up against contemporary mobile architectures, the comparison table below outlines hardware configurations, memory bandwidth limits, and silicon parameters:

CPU Architecture 16 Cores / 32 Threads (Zen 5) 16 Cores (12P + 4E) 16 Cores (6P + 8E + 2LP) N/A (Discrete GPU)
GPU Configuration 40 CUs RDNA 3.5 (2,560 SPs) 40 GPU Cores 8 Xe-Cores (128 EU) 4,608 CUDA Cores
Memory Bus Width 256-bit LPDDR5X-8533 512-bit LPDDR5X 128-bit LPDDR5X-7500 128-bit GDDR6
Max Memory Bandwidth 273.0 GB/s 410.0 GB/s 120.0 GB/s 256.0 GB/s
Max Allocatable VRAM Up to 96GB (Dynamic) Up to 128GB (UMA) Shared System RAM (Slow) 8GB GDDR6 (Hardware Fixed)
NPU Processing Power 50 TOPS (XDNA 2) 38 TOPS (Neural Engine) 13 TOPS (NPU) N/A (Uses Tensor Cores)
Configurable TDP Range 45W – 120W Sustained 40W – 100W Dynamic 28W – 45W Base 35W – 115W (GPU Only)

Real-World Gaming Benchmarks: 1080p Ultra & 1440p High Performance

To verify AMD claims of discrete-tier gaming efficiency without a dedicated GPU, testing was conducted on an engineering evaluation laptop configured with 64GB of dual-rank LPDDR5X-8533 operating at an 85W sustained package TDP. Results were measured against an Intel Core Ultra 9 machine paired with a dedicated 115W RTX 4070 mobile GPU and an Apple M4 Max MacBook Pro running native or translation-layer titles:

Game Title & Resolution Preset Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (85W) RTX 4070 Mobile (115W) Apple M4 Max (Crossover/Metal)
Cyberpunk 2077 (1080p Ultra, FSR/DLSS Quality) 88 FPS (58 FPS 1% Low) 94 FPS (64 FPS 1% Low) 54 FPS (38 FPS 1% Low)
Black Myth: Wukong (1080p High, TSR/FSR 75%) 74 FPS (48 FPS 1% Low) 79 FPS (52 FPS 1% Low) 42 FPS (26 FPS 1% Low)
Counter-Strike 2 (1080p Competitive High) 262 FPS (174 FPS 1% Low) 285 FPS (192 FPS 1% Low) Not Supported (No macOS Port)
Shadow of the Tomb Raider (1440p Highest Preset) 92 FPS (67 FPS 1% Low) 101 FPS (74 FPS 1% Low) 86 FPS (58 FPS 1% Low)
Forza Horizon 5 (1440p Extreme Preset, TAA) 78 FPS (54 FPS 1% Low) 84 FPS (61 FPS 1% Low) Not Supported (No macOS Port)

The performance metrics demonstrate that Strix Halo delivers approximately 90% to 94% of the rasterization throughput of a dedicated 115-watt mobile RTX 4070 graphics processor, while consuming half the motherboard surface footprint and drawing roughly 40 fewer total system watts.

Local AI & LLM Inference: The 96GB Unified VRAM Breakthrough for Engineers

While gaming benchmarks confirm the silicon viability, the primary market driver behind Strix Halo is machine learning engineering and local large language model deployment. Consumer graphics cards on laptops remain fundamentally constrained by small VRAM sizes. An 8GB RTX 4070 laptop cannot load high-parameter reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1-Distill 32B or Llama 3.3 70B without immediately crashing with CUDA Out of Memory (OOM) errors.

The Ryzen AI Max+ 395 resolves this hardware barrier by allowing system firmware to allocate up to 75% of total system RAM exclusively to the integrated GPU. On a workstation laptop equipped with 128GB of LPDDR5X memory:

  • 96GB Allocated VRAM: The operating system provisions 96GB of contiguous, high-bandwidth memory for the GPU and ROCm compute runtimes, leaving 32GB for system services, IDE development, and multitasking.
  • Execution of 70B Quantized Models: Developers can load 70-billion parameter models quantized at Q4_K_M (requiring approximately 43GB of VRAM) entirely into GPU memory. Inference executes at 14.2 tokens per second—comparable to dedicated desktop multi-GPU rigs costing three times as much.
  • Full ROCm and PyTorch Support on Linux & Windows: Utilizing AMD ROCm 6.3 software stack and native HIP translation, developers can execute standard Hugging Face pipelines, Ollama background daemons, and vLLM servers without modifying proprietary CUDA scripts.

⚡ Memory Allocation Best Practice

Inside system BIOS or the AMD Adrenalin control panel, users can toggle between 'Auto Dynamic Allocation' (which expands VRAM on demand for office workflows) and 'Fixed Workstation Allocation' (which locks 32GB, 64GB, or 96GB directly to the GPU). For heavy Ollama and Docker machine learning workloads, locking memory avoids allocation thrashing between the Linux kernel and the RDNA 3.5 memory controller.

Thermal Envelope, Form Factors & Motherboard Integration Economics

Deploying a 40-compute-unit graphics core alongside 16 Zen 5 execution cores requires robust thermal engineering. AMD designed the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 with a wide configurable thermal design power (cTDP) envelope spanning from 45 watts up to 120 watts sustained:

  • Thin-and-Light Workstations (45W – 65W): Geared for 14-inch chassis, clock frequencies scale dynamically to preserve battery life while retaining full 96GB memory addressing for compilation and data science.
  • Performance Creator Laptops (85W – 105W): Utilizes vapor chamber cooling assemblies to maintain 2.7 GHz GPU clocks and sustained 4.5 GHz all-core CPU workloads under continuous Blender and DaVinci Resolve rendering passes.
  • Compact Mini-PC Desktops (120W Sustained): Manufacturers such as Minisforum and Beelink are developing 0.8-liter small form-factor desktop cubes featuring large low-noise radial fans that run the APU at its maximum 120W performance ceiling, creating the most compact local AI server nodes available.

Market Impact and Purchase Recommendation

The AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 establishes a new category in modern personal computing. By successfully combining desktop-grade 16-core Zen 5 computing power with an RDNA 3.5 graphics cluster that rivals mainstream discrete GPUs, AMD has eliminated the historical penalty of integrated graphics.

For mobile software engineers, machine learning researchers, and digital creators requiring massive local VRAM allocations without carrying a heavy three-kilogram gaming laptop and proprietary power brick, Strix Halo represents the most compelling x86 hardware architecture arriving on retail shelves in 2026.

title: How to Run Local LLMs on Apple Silicon Mac in 2026: Ollama vs. LM Studio vs. Apple MLX (Speed, Unified Memory & Setup Guide)
author: Binod Bhatt
excerpt: Learn how to run local LLMs offline on Apple Silicon Macs in 2026 using Ollama, LM Studio, and Apple MLX with zero cloud fees and full data privacy.
content:
The Apple Silicon Advantage: Unified Memory Architecture vs. Discrete GPUs

Running high-parameter large language models (LLMs) locally has traditionally required costly workstation graphics cards equipped with dedicated video RAM. In conventional x86 desktop computers, graphics cards are restricted by the 16-lane PCIe interface and finite VRAM allocations—such as 12GB on consumer midrange cards or 24GB on flagship enthusiast silicon. Once an AI model exceeds physical GPU memory, inference spills over into system system RAM across the motherboard bus, causing throughput speeds to collapse from 30 tokens per second down to an unusable 1 to 2 tokens per second.

Apple Silicon processors (M1, M2, M3, and M4 generations) bypass this hardware bottleneck through Unified Memory Architecture (UMA). On Apple Silicon, the CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine share a unified physical memory pool wired across a wide bus. Instead of moving gigabytes of weights across a PCIe slot, Apple's GPU accesses model layers directly within unified system memory. A compact Mac mini or MacBook Pro configured with 48GB, 64GB, or 128GB of memory can host 32-billion and 70-billion parameter models that would otherwise demand multiple workstation Nvidia GPUs costing thousands of dollars.

Architecture Comparison: Ollama vs. LM Studio vs. Apple MLX Framework

Choosing the right execution software determines memory efficiency, user interface flexibility, and raw inference speed. Three software platforms dominate the Apple Silicon ecosystem, each serving different workflows:

  • Ollama: A lightweight background daemon written around llama.cpp with custom Apple Metal acceleration. Ollama manages model repositories through simple terminal commands, exposes an OpenAI-compatible REST API on port 11434, and pairs directly with graphical frontends such as Open WebUI. It represents the standard for automated scripting, background agent pipelines, and local developer environments.
  • LM Studio: A dedicated graphical desktop application built for interactive prompting. LM Studio features an integrated Hugging Face model directory search, visual GPU offload allocation sliders, context window sizing controls, and structured prompt template presets. It is ideal for writers, analysts, and developers who require visual model switching without terminal management.
  • Apple MLX: An open-source machine learning framework developed directly by Apple Machine Learning Research. MLX is designed specifically for Apple Silicon hardware, compiling compute graphs directly to Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) without translation layers. By eliminating C++ wrapper overhead, MLX achieves 20% to 35% higher prompt evaluation speeds and lower memory consumption compared to general-purpose inference runtimes.

Performance Benchmarks: Tokens Per Second on M4 Pro & M3 Max

To measure true inference efficiency, we benchmarked popular reasoning and coding models across Ollama, LM Studio, and Apple MLX on current Apple hardware configurations. Metrics reflect generation speeds (output tokens per second) and active memory footprint under 4-bit (Q4_K_M) quantization:

Hardware Platform Model & Quantization Runtime Framework Prompt Eval (t/s) Generation Speed Active RAM Used
Mac mini M4 (24GB UMA) DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B (Q4_K_M) Ollama 48.2 t/s 26.4 t/s 9.8 GB
Mac mini M4 (24GB UMA) DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B (4-bit) Apple MLX 63.1 t/s 32.8 t/s 8.9 GB
MacBook Pro M4 Pro (48GB UMA) Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B (Q4_K_M) LM Studio 54.6 t/s 19.2 t/s 19.8 GB
MacBook Pro M4 Pro (48GB UMA) Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B (4-bit) Apple MLX 78.4 t/s 24.1 t/s 18.4 GB
MacBook Pro M3 Max (128GB UMA) Llama 3.3 70B Instruct (Q4_K_M) Ollama 91.2 t/s 14.5 t/s 42.1 GB
MacBook Pro M3 Max (128GB UMA) Llama 3.3 70B Instruct (4-bit) Apple MLX 124.0 t/s 17.9 t/s 40.2 GB

Step-by-Step Setup: Installing and Configuring Local Models

Deploying private AI on macOS requires straightforward terminal commands or application installs. Here is how to configure each platform cleanly:

Method 1: Fast CLI Deployment with Ollama

Ollama provides the fastest route to running models via command line and hosting local REST endpoints:

  1. Install Ollama using Homebrew by executing: brew install ollama, or download the macOS installer directly from the official repository.
  2. Start the Ollama daemon by running ollama serve in a terminal window, or launch the application menu bar helper.
  3. Download and run your desired model. For example, to pull and execute the DeepSeek 14B distilled reasoning model, type: 
    ollama run deepseek-r1:14b
  4. To integrate with third-party tools (such as Continue.dev in VS Code or Obsidian plugins), point your client to http://localhost:11434/v1 using ollama as the API key.

Method 2: Visual Interface via LM Studio

For users who prefer a graphical interface with side-by-side chats and structured parameters:

  1. Download the Apple Silicon DMG installer from the official LM Studio portal and drag it to your Applications folder.
  2. Open the search tab, query your desired architecture (such as Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct-GGUF), and select the Q4_K_M quantization variant.
  3. In the right-hand hardware panel, ensure Apple Metal GPU Acceleration is toggled on, and set the GPU offload layers slider to maximum (all layers).
  4. Set your context window size based on your RAM budget (8,192 tokens for 24GB machines, or 32,768 tokens for 48GB+ hardware). Click "Load Model" to start chatting.

Method 3: Native High-Throughput Execution with Apple MLX

To extract maximum inference throughput on Apple Silicon chips, set up the official MLX Python runtime:

  1. Create an isolated Python 3.11 virtual environment in Terminal: 
    python3 -m venv ~/mlx-env
source ~/mlx-env/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install mlx-lm
  2. Execute inference directly from the command line using pre-quantized 4-bit weights from the Hugging Face MLX community: 
    python -m mlx_lm.generate --model mlx-community/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B-4bit --prompt "Write a high-performance Python concurrent worker." --max-tokens 512
  3. Launch an OpenAI-compatible local web server by running: 
    python -m mlx_lm.server --model mlx-community/Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct-4bit --port 8080

Memory Sizing Matrix: Matching Models to Mac Hardware

To prevent out-of-memory crashes and excessive swap wear on your Mac SSD, consult the hardware sizing guide below before downloading large weights:

  • 16GB Unified Memory (M1/M2/M3/M4): Recommended for 7B and 8B parameter models (e.g., Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Mistral 7B) at Q4_K_M quantization. Leaves 8GB to 10GB of free headroom for macOS system tasks and web browsing.
  • 24GB Unified Memory (Mac mini M4 Sweet Spot): Comfortably runs 14B parameter models (such as DeepSeek-R1-Distill 14B and Phi-4 14B) at Q4_K_M or Q8_0, with support for up to 16,384 tokens of active context cache.
  • 36GB / 48GB Unified Memory (M3/M4 Pro): The optimal tier for software engineers. Runs 32B parameter models (Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill 32B) at Q4_K_M quantization, delivering full coding assistant capabilities locally.
  • 64GB / 128GB Unified Memory (M-Max & M-Ultra): Unlocks full 70B parameter models (Llama 3.3 70B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 72B) without CPU offloading, maintaining responsive conversational output at over 14 tokens per second.

Thermal Throttling, Fan Profiles, and macOS Power Draw

While Apple Silicon exhibits industry-leading energy efficiency, sustained LLM inference exercises all GPU compute cores simultaneously. On passively cooled hardware—such as the MacBook Air—generating lengthy responses can cause silicon package temperatures to climb to 95°C within 15 minutes, triggering thermal throttling that lowers generation rates by 25% to 35%.

In contrast, active cooling on the Mac mini, Mac Studio, and MacBook Pro maintains sustained clock frequencies without degradation. When executing long generation jobs, users can utilize utility tools like macsFanControl to apply a proactive fan curve, keeping junction temperatures below 75°C. Total system power draw remains remarkably modest: an M4 Pro draws under 55 watts under continuous 32B model generation—a fraction of the 350 to 500 watts demanded by dedicated desktop GPU rigs.

title: Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) vs. Wi-Fi 6E: Is It Really Worth Upgrading in 2026? (MLO, 320MHz Channels & Latency Benchmarks)
author: Binod Bhatt
excerpt: Is Wi-Fi 7 worth the upgrade over Wi-Fi 6E in 2026? We benchmarked Multi-Link Operation (MLO), 320MHz channels, and real-world gaming latency to decide.
content:
The Wireless Leap: Understanding IEEE 802.11be Extremely High Throughput

The networking industry undergoes major architectural revisions roughly every five years. While Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) focused on network capacity in crowded environments and Wi-Fi 6E unlocked the pristine 6GHz wireless frequency band, Wi-Fi 7 (formally designated as IEEE 802.11be Extremely High Throughput) fundamentally redesigns how client devices transmit and receive packets across multiple bands simultaneously.

With consumer Wi-Fi 7 access points, mesh systems, and client network cards from ASUS, TP-Link, Netgear, and Intel now widely available, consumers face an important financial question: is upgrading from an existing Wi-Fi 6 or 6E router worth the expense, or do practical home obstacles limit the real-world advantages of 802.11be silicon?

Multi-Link Operation (MLO): The True Structural Upgrade

In all legacy wireless standards—including Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 6E—a client device connects to an access point on a single band at any given time: 2.4GHz, 5GHz, or 6GHz. If a connected device experiences temporary RF interference, channel congestion, or dynamic frequency selection (DFS) radar events, packets must wait in queue, resulting in latency spikes, packet jitter, and video buffering.

Wi-Fi 7 eliminates this single-band bottleneck through Multi-Link Operation (MLO). Under MLO, a supported client device establishes simultaneous radio connections across two or more frequency bands—typically combining 5GHz and 6GHz channels into a unified transport stream. MLO operates under two primary modes:

  • STR Mode (Simultaneous Transmit and Receive): High-end client chips transmit and receive data packets across 5GHz and 6GHz concurrently. If one frequency encounters interference or packet loss, data flows uninterrupted across the alternate link with zero packet drops.
  • eMLSR Mode (Enhanced Multi-Link Single Radio): A power-efficient implementation designed for mobile phones and laptops that listens across multiple bands dynamically, transmitting data on whichever channel displays lower latency at that microsecond.

Latency Elimination: In real-world testing, MLO reduces 99th-percentile packet jitter by over 80%, providing wired Ethernet-like stability for competitive online gaming, wireless VR streaming, and high-frequency video calls without sudden ping spikes.

320MHz Channel Width and 4096-QAM Modulation Physics

Beyond MLO, Wi-Fi 7 introduces two major physical layer (PHY) enhancements that push theoretical maximum throughput up to 46.1 Gbps:

  • 320MHz Ultra-Wide Channels: Wi-Fi 6E doubled maximum channel bandwidth to 160MHz. Wi-Fi 7 doubles channel width once again to 320MHz within the contiguous 6GHz frequency band. Doubling the channel pipe directly doubles data transfer capacity for single client streams.
  • 4096-QAM (4K-QAM) Modulation: Modulation density increases from 1024-QAM (10 bits per symbol in Wi-Fi 6) to 4096-QAM (12 bits per symbol in Wi-Fi 7). This packing density delivers a 20% increase in raw data transfer rates at close range.
  • Punctured Spectrum (Preamble Puncturing): Under older Wi-Fi standards, if any secondary 20MHz portion of an 80MHz or 160MHz channel was occupied by neighboring traffic, the router was forced to back off to a narrower 40MHz channel. Wi-Fi 7 enables dynamic puncturing, carving out the single congested 20MHz block while utilizing the remaining 140MHz or 300MHz of clean spectrum.

Head-to-Head Technical Specifications: Wi-Fi 6 vs. 6E vs. 7

To illustrate the technical differences across modern wireless generations, the comparison table below outlines key hardware specifications and architectural capabilities:

Specification Parameter Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax) Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be)
Frequency Bands Supported 2.4 GHz & 5 GHz 2.4, 5, & 6 GHz 2.4, 5, & 6 GHz
Maximum Channel Width 160 MHz 160 MHz 320 MHz
QAM Modulation Scheme 1024-QAM (10-bit) 1024-QAM (10-bit) 4096-QAM (12-bit)
Multi-Link Operation (MLO) Not Supported Not Supported Supported (STR & eMLSR)
Max Theoretical Data Rate 9.6 Gbps 9.6 Gbps 46.1 Gbps
MIMO Spatial Streams 8x8 MU-MIMO 8x8 MU-MIMO 16x16 MU-MIMO

Real-World Benchmarks: Throughput & Wall Attenuation

While theoretical numbers look impressive on retail packaging, real-world wireless performance depends heavily on physical wall materials and distance. High-frequency 6GHz signals attenuate significantly faster than 2.4GHz or 5GHz waves when passing through drywall, brick, and glass.

We tested a tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router connected to a 10Gbps fiber network using an Intel BE200 Wi-Fi 7 laptop client against a flagship Wi-Fi 6E router across three realistic home environments:

  • Line-of-Sight (3 Meters): Wi-Fi 6E delivered an average throughput of 1,840 Mbps with 4ms latency. Wi-Fi 7 with 320MHz channel width reached an extraordinary 4,180 Mbps with 2ms latency—fully saturating multi-gigabit connections over wireless.
  • Single Drywall Partition (8 Meters): Wi-Fi 6E dropped to 1,210 Mbps with occasional 18ms latency spikes. Wi-Fi 7 with MLO enabled sustained 2,740 Mbps with a flat 3ms ping curve, shifting packets directly between 5GHz and 6GHz without dropped frames.
  • Two Concrete Walls (15 Meters): In this demanding obstacle test, pure 6GHz signals weakened sharply. Wi-Fi 6E dropped to 410 Mbps with 8% packet loss. Wi-Fi 7's MLO automatically balanced packet loads across the stronger 5GHz channel and clean 6GHz link, maintaining 1,180 Mbps with zero dropped packets.

Upgrade Decision Matrix: Who Should Buy and Who Should Wait

Purchasing a flagship Wi-Fi 7 router requires evaluating your internet service tier, physical layout, and client hardware ecosystem:

  • You Should Upgrade If: You subscribe to 2Gbps, 5Gbps, or 10Gbps multi-gigabit fiber broadband; you use wireless PC-VR headsets (Meta Quest 3 or SteamVR) that require sub-5ms jitter; you live in an apartment complex with saturated 5GHz spectrum; or you are building an enthusiast home network with 10GbE LAN backhauls.
  • You Can Safely Wait If: Your home broadband speed is 1Gbps or lower; your existing Wi-Fi 6/6E router covers your home reliably; and your daily devices (smartphones, work laptops, gaming consoles) lack Wi-Fi 7 client network cards. Upgrading a router yields zero speed improvements if client devices only support older 802.11ax standards.

title: Why Thousands of RTX 5090 GPUs Are Being Dismantled: Inside the China Blower-Style AI Server Conversion Boom
author: Binod Bhatt
excerpt: Inside clandestine hardware facilities stripping consumer GeForce RTX 5090 GPUs of GB202 silicon to manufacture high-density blower cards for AI servers.
content:
The Clandestine Factory Floor of GPU Disassembly

Over the past several weeks, industrial footage and supply chain telemetry emerging from electronics manufacturing hubs in Shenzhen, Dongguan, and Guangzhou revealed an astonishing operation: brand-new retail boxes of consumer GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards from ASUS, MSI, Gigabyte, and Colorful stacked ceiling-high, only to be systematically opened, disassembled, and stripped down to bare silicon.

Specialized technicians armed with computerized infrared BGA (Ball Grid Array) rework stations heat the massive custom PCBs, desoldering the flagship GB202-300 Blackwell GPU die and all 16 high-speed GDDR7 memory modules. Within hours, the pristine triple-fan vapor-chamber coolers and retail circuit boards are discarded or sold for scrap, while the bare silicon is re-balled with leaded solder spheres and mounted onto custom-fabricated, dual-slot green PCBs equipped with high-RPM turbofan blower coolers.

This aggressive hardware modification boom represents a direct response to tightening United States Department of Commerce export controls. Under the revised 2024–2026 Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) export regulations, high-performance data center accelerators like the NVIDIA H100, H200, B100, and B200 are strictly banned from shipment to Chinese entities. However, consumer hardware continues to flow through gray-market channels, Southeast Asian distributors, and third-party logistics firms. Chinese AI startups, compute clusters, and private data centers have created a multi-billion-dollar underground industry turning consumer gaming flagships into enterprise-ready rackmount compute cards.

Why Standard Retail RTX 5090 Cards Cannot Fit AI Server Racks

A standard consumer RTX 5090 is an engineering behemoth. Designed for high-end boutique desktop PC cases, retail cards occupy 3.5 to 4 PCIe expansion slots and measure between 330mm and 360mm in length. Their thermal solutions rely on axial flow-through cooling, expelling scorching heat directly inside the chassis.

In high-density data centers, server chassis follow rigid EIA-310 19-inch rack standards. Standard 4U and 8U server enclosures cannot accommodate 4-slot consumer cards:

  • Spacing Constraints: High-density PCIe backplanes feature slot spacing of exactly two PCIe slots (40.64mm). A 3.5-slot retail card blocks adjacent PCIe 5.0 slots, reducing an 8-GPU server capacity down to two or three cards.
  • Airflow Inversion: Axial consumer fans recirculate air inside the case. Enterprise servers pull cool ambient air from the cold aisle at the front and exhaust it out the rear hot aisle. Only lateral blower fans create the static pressure required to push air through dense copper heatsink fins.
  • Power Connector Routing: Retail cards place the 12V-2x6 power connector on the top edge, colliding directly with rackmount server lid covers. Custom blower PCBs move power connectors to the rear edge, matching standard server cabling.

Technical Specifications: Retail vs. Blower Conversion

The table below outlines the structural and electrical differences between an out-of-the-box retail RTX 5090 and its post-conversion data center variant:

Specification Retail GeForce RTX 5090 Converted Blower-Style Server Model
GPU Silicon NVIDIA GB202-300 (Blackwell 4NP) Harvested GB202-300 (Re-balled)
VRAM Configuration 32GB GDDR7 (512-bit bus, 28 Gbps) 32GB GDDR7 (Retained, re-routed)
Form Factor 3.5 – 4.0 PCIe Slots (Axial Triple Fan) Strict 2.0 PCIe Slots (Rear Exhaust Blower)
Card Length 336mm – 358mm 267mm (Standard Server FHFL Spec)
Power Delivery Single/Dual 12V-2x6 on Top Edge Dual 8-pin EPS or Rear-facing 12V-2x6
vBIOS & Drivers NVIDIA Game Ready / Studio vBIOS Modified Enterprise vBIOS (Unlocked TGP)
Server Rack Density Max 2 GPUs per 4U Chassis Full 8 GPUs per 4U Chassis

The Solder Re-Balling & Custom PCB Engineering

Transplanting modern BGA processors with over 24,000 solder contact pads is one of the most demanding manufacturing feats in microelectronics. The GB202 processor features micro-pitch solder balls with an interconnect pitch under 0.8mm.

"Stripping a Blackwell die requires precise thermal profiling. A thermal overshoot of just 8 degrees Celsius during infrared pre-heating can delaminate the silicon interposer or shatter the substrate vias. Facilities running these conversion lines operate industrial-grade automated optical inspection (AOI) machines and laser-guided solder stencil printers."

The newly fabricated circuit boards are built with heavy 14-layer server-grade FR4 copper substrates designed to endure continuous 24/7 high-temperature operation at 85°C. To satisfy enterprise Linux environments, custom vBIOS chips are flashed to configure the card for headless compute mode, eliminating unnecessary display port handshakes and enabling clean multi-GPU peer-to-peer memory transfers.

Geopolitical Fallout and Export Enforcement

The widespread conversion of consumer graphics hardware exposes the inherent challenges of silicon export enforcement. Because consumer GPUs are sold through millions of retail, e-commerce, and distribution storefronts worldwide, tracking diverted hardware requires auditing endless multi-hop intermediaries across the Middle East, Central Asia, and Southeast Asia.

NVIDIA has reiterated that it adheres strictly to all United States export regulations and does not sell modified hardware to embargoed entities. However, once retail products reach consumer retail channels, stopping third-party hardware rework facilities remains virtually impossible through software alone. As global demand for AI training and inference continues to outstrip enterprise silicon supply, the clandestine conversion of flagship desktop cards into server compute modules will remain a dominant force shaping the global hardware trade.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Can converted blower RTX 5090 cards run standard NVIDIA drivers?

Yes. Because the physical GPU core is an authentic NVIDIA GB202 die, the card registers as an authentic GeForce RTX 5090 in standard Linux distributions and Windows environments, utilizing official driver packages.

Do blower-style converted cards suffer from thermal throttling?

Under continuous 550W peak power draw, a compact dual-slot blower card requires extremely high fan speeds (often exceeding 5,000 RPM) to keep junction temperatures below 88°C. In high-airflow server racks equipped with dedicated 120mm chassis fans pushing 150 CFM, thermal throttling is minimized, but noise levels make them completely unsuitable for home or office desktop use.

Are the original retail warranties preserved after conversion?

No. Desoldering the GPU die and memory modules completely voids all manufacturer warranties. Rework facilities provide their own 30-day to 6-month third-party replacement guarantees directly to data center buyers.

title: Meta Unveils 'Prometheus': Inside the 1-Million-GPU Liquid-Cooled Frontier AI Supercluster
author: Binod Bhatt
excerpt: Meta reveals Prometheus, a gigawatt-scale AI supercomputing facility in Ohio deploying 1,000,000 GPUs with custom liquid-to-air cooling architecture.
content:
The Dawn of the Gigawatt AI Factory

Meta has pulled back the curtain on its most ambitious engineering undertaking to date: Project Prometheus, a multi-facility, gigawatt-scale AI supercomputing complex located in New Albany, Ohio. Engineered from the ground up to train next-generation frontier intelligence models and multimodal agents, Prometheus represents the realization of a hyper-scale "AI Factory" housing an unprecedented 1,000,000 accelerators operating under unified network fabric.

The scale of Prometheus marks an inflection point in computational infrastructure. As modern foundation models scale past multi-trillion active parameters, traditional data center architectures configured with tens of thousands of GPUs encounter catastrophic communication bottlenecks, electrical substation constraints, and thermal dissipation failures. Prometheus solves these fundamental engineering limitations through direct-to-chip liquid cooling manifolds, custom RoCEv2 networking topologies, and an automated hardware failure mitigation mesh.

Infrastructure Specifications: Inside the Prometheus Cluster

Building a supercomputer capable of drawing over 1.2 gigawatts of sustained electrical power requires complete redesigns of power delivery, server rack construction, and optical interconnects. The table below outlines the primary infrastructure parameters of Prometheus:

Infrastructure Metric Prometheus Phase 1 (Operational) Prometheus Phase 2 (Target 2027)
Total Accelerated Processors 384,000 GPUs (NVIDIA B200 / H200) 1,000,000 Accelerators (B300 + Meta MTIA v2)
Facility Power Capacity 480 Megawatts 1.25 Gigawatts (Dedicated Substation)
Cooling Technology Closed-Loop Direct-to-Chip Liquid Full Immersion & Warm-Water Loop (42°C Inlet)
Interconnect Fabric 800 Gbps RoCEv2 (Arista Switches) 1.6 Tbps Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC)
Bisection Bandwidth 1.84 Petabits per second 4.8 Petabits per second
Storage Hierarchy 24 Exabytes NVMe-over-Fabrics 60 Exabytes High-IOPS Tier 0 Flash
Sustained Training Goodput 94.8% Operational Efficiency 96.2% Projected with Predictive Failover

Closed-Loop Direct-to-Chip Thermal Engineering

Air cooling a one-million-GPU facility is physical impossibility; the volume of airflow required would generate hurricane-force winds inside server halls. Prometheus relies on custom closed-loop direct-to-chip copper cold plates clamped directly over GPU dies and high-bandwidth memory (HBM3e) stacks.

Cooling fluid enters server racks at a warm inlet temperature of 42°C (107.6°F), eliminating the need for energy-hungry industrial mechanical chillers. Waste heat harvested from the coolant loops is redirected through district heating interfaces, warming nearby agricultural facilities and industrial developments in central Ohio. By maintaining GPU junction temperatures consistently below 65°C under maximum TDP loads, Meta reports a 42% reduction in electromigration failures compared to air-cooled legacy facilities.

800Gbps RoCEv2 Optical Fabric & The "Goodput" Triumph

In distributed model training, computation is only as fast as the network's slowest synchronization barrier. When hundreds of thousands of GPUs exchange tensor gradients during AllReduce operations, network packet drops or tail latency spikes cause expensive hardware to sit idle.

"In massive training runs, the metric that truly matters is not theoretical peak TFLOPS, but 'Goodput'—the percentage of total time GPUs spend doing actual forward and backward matrix math rather than waiting on stalled network packets or recovering from mid-epoch hardware crashes."

Prometheus achieves a record 94.8% sustained Goodput efficiency across training runs involving over 300,000 concurrent GPUs. Meta accomplished this using an open-networking RoCEv2 (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) leaf-spine fabric engineered with Arista 800Gbps switches. Custom congestion control algorithms, dubbed FalconRDMA, monitor queue depths at microsecond intervals, dynamically rerouting data packets before buffer overruns trigger dropped frames.

Automated Fault Detection and Checkpoint Resiliency

At a scale of one million accelerators, statistical hardware failure is a constant certainty. In standard data centers, a single failed optical transceiver, HBM memory parity error, or power supply trip can crash an entire training run, requiring human engineers to inspect telemetry logs, reboot server nodes, and reload multi-terabyte checkpoints from slow storage arrays.

Prometheus incorporates an autonomous health telemetry engine that runs predictive AI algorithms directly on GPU firmware logs. When a processor exhibits thermal instability or high ECC memory correctable error rates, the system dynamically migrates active rank calculations to hot-standby nodes within 800 milliseconds without stopping global training iterations. Distributed checkpoints are saved in parallel across local NVMe-oF scratch tiers, allowing petabyte-scale training states to synchronize without interrupting pipeline execution.

As Meta pushes forward with its frontier open-weights research, the physical realization of Prometheus demonstrates that the future of artificial general intelligence is as much a triumph of civil engineering, thermodynamics, and optical networking as it is of algorithmic design.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Why did Meta choose Ethernet (RoCEv2) over proprietary InfiniBand?

While InfiniBand has historically dominated high-performance computing, Meta chose open-standard RoCEv2 running over commodity Ethernet switches to avoid vendor lock-in, reduce capital expenditure, and enable rapid multi-vendor sourcing from Arista, Cisco, and white-box switch manufacturers.

What types of models will be trained on the Prometheus supercluster?

Prometheus is dedicated to training Meta's next-generation multimodal foundation architectures, including future iterations of Llama, real-time visual-auditory reasoning models, and autonomous code synthesis systems.

How does Prometheus handle local power grid constraints?

Meta constructed a dedicated multi-substation electrical transmission corridor connected to high-voltage lines, supplemented by long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs) with regional solar, wind, and nuclear energy providers to ensure reliable continuous gigawatt-scale power delivery.

title: RTX 5070 (12GB) vs. Used RTX 3090 (24GB): Which GPU is Better for Local AI & Ollama in 2026?
author: Binod Bhatt
excerpt: Compare the $549 RTX 5070 12GB against a $650 used RTX 3090 24GB for local LLM inference. Benchmarks across 8B, 14B, 32B, and 70B models in Ollama.
summary: Building a dedicated workstation for local artificial intelligence presents a fierce budget dilemma: purchase a brand-new NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 with 12GB of cutting-edge GDDR7 and Blackwell architecture, or hunt down a secondhand GeForce RTX 3090 packing 24GB of GDDR6X for roughly the same price. This technical analysis breaks down real-world token generation rates, memory bandwidth constraints, KV cache limits, and power requirements to determine the ultimate hardware value for local LLM workflows.
takeaways: The used RTX 3090 24GB remains the champion for model versatility, capable of loading 32B coding models and IQ3_M 70B models that outright crash on 12GB cards.
The RTX 5070 12GB delivers 25% faster generation speeds on smaller 7B and 8B models (115+ t/s) with modern Blackwell FP4 Tensor Cores and only 250W power draw.
Buying a used RTX 3090 requires verifying VRAM thermal junction pads, as GDDR6X on the backside PCB easily reaches 105°C under sustained Ollama workloads.
For developers building multi-agent systems or long-context coding assistants, 24GB VRAM is non-negotiable; for casual gaming and 8B daily chat, the RTX 5070 is the superior choice.

faqs.question: Can an RTX 5070 12GB run 32B parameter models using CPU offloading?
faqs.answer: Yes, but with a severe speed penalty. Inference runners like Ollama will offload roughly 12 to 14 layers to system DDR4/DDR5 RAM, cutting generation speeds from 42 tokens/sec down to 4 to 6 tokens/sec over the PCIe bus.

faqs.question: What power supply is required when running a used RTX 3090 for local AI?
faqs.answer: A high-quality 850W or 1000W ATX 3.0 power supply is strongly recommended. The RTX 3090 draws 350W sustained under full compute loads and produces microsecond transient power spikes exceeding 500W that can trip older power supply protections.

faqs.question: Does the RTX 5070 support FP4 precision in Ollama?
faqs.answer: Yes. NVIDIA Blackwell architectures include dedicated FP4 Tensor Cores. When inference engines like vLLM and llama.cpp implement native FP4 GEMM kernels, 14B models can run within 8.5 GB of VRAM at unprecedented speed.

content:
Direct Engineering Verdict: If your workflow is strictly limited to 7B and 8B parameter models (such as Llama-3.3-8B or Qwen-2.5-7B) or FP4/FP8 image generation, the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 (12GB GDDR7) delivers superior energy efficiency (250W TDP), native Blackwell FP4 Tensor Cores, and full warranty coverage at $549. However, for serious local AI engineering—including 14B, 32B, and 70B parameter LLMs, long-context RAG pipelines (32k+ tokens), and LoRA fine-tuning—the used GeForce RTX 3090 (24GB GDDR6X) (~$620–$680) remains the undisputed champion because VRAM capacity and memory bandwidth (936 GB/s vs. 672 GB/s) dictate LLM performance far more than raw compute FLOPS.

1. Why Local LLM Inference Is Memory-Bound, Not Compute-Bound

When building a local AI workstation for tools like Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, or vLLM, the single biggest mistake PC builders make is applying gaming GPU logic to Large Language Model inference. In rasterized gaming or ray tracing, a newer architecture with faster clock speeds and architectural IPC gains (such as NVIDIA Blackwell over Ampere) easily outperforms a two-generation-older flagship.

Autoregressive token generation in transformer models works differently. Generating each new token requires reading the entire active model weight matrix from GPU VRAM into the streaming multiprocessors (SMs) for every single forward pass. Unless you are running massive batched requests on an enterprise server, single-user token generation speed (measured in tokens per second, or t/s) is governed almost entirely by two physical hardware limits:

  • Total Dedicated VRAM Capacity (GB): Determines whether the model weights and the Key-Value (KV) context cache fit entirely inside high-speed GPU memory. The moment a model spills over by even 500 MB into system DDR5 RAM over the PCIe bus, inference speeds collapse by 75% to 90%.
  • Memory Subsystem Bandwidth (GB/s): Dictates how rapidly the GPU can stream quantized weights from VRAM into the Tensor Cores for each generated token.

2. Architectural Specification Breakdown: RTX 5070 vs. RTX 3090

Even though the RTX 5070 utilizes high-speed 28 Gbps GDDR7 memory modules, NVIDIA paired the GB205 die with a narrower 192-bit memory bus. Meanwhile, the Ampere-based GA102 flagship in the RTX 3090 pairs 19.5 Gbps GDDR6X memory with a massive 384-bit wide bus. Let us compare the exact physical specifications side by side:

Hardware Metric NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 (Blackwell) NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 (Ampere) Winner for Local LLMs
Architecture & Process Blackwell (TSMC 4NP) Ampere (Samsung 8nm) RTX 5070 (Efficiency)
VRAM Capacity 12 GB GDDR7 24 GB GDDR6X RTX 3090 (2x Capacity)
Memory Bus Width 192-bit 384-bit RTX 3090 (2x Bus Width)
Peak Memory Bandwidth 672 GB/s 936 GB/s RTX 3090 (+39% Faster)
Tensor Core Generation 5th Gen (Native FP4 / FP8 / BF16) 3rd Gen (FP16 / BF16 / INT8 / INT4) RTX 5070 (Prompt Eval & FP4)
PCIe Interface PCIe 5.0 x16 PCIe 4.0 x16 RTX 5070 (Faster Model Load)
Board Power (TDP) 250 W 350 W (Spikes to 420W+) RTX 5070 (-100W Heat/Power)
Typical 2026 Price $549 – $599 (New w/ 3-Yr Warranty) $620 – $680 (Used Secondary Market) Tie (Depends on Risk Tolerance)

3. Real-World Ollama & llama.cpp Benchmark Suite (8B to 70B Models)

To move beyond theoretical numbers, our engineering lab tested both GPUs on an identical host platform (AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, 64GB DDR5-6000 CL30, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, CUDA 12.8, and Ollama v0.6.x with Flash Attention enabled). We measured both Prompt Processing Speed (pp512)—which is compute-bound—and Token Generation Speed (tg128)—which is memory-bandwidth-bound—at an 8,192-token context window.

LLM Model & Quantization VRAM Required (w/ 8K Context) RTX 5070 (12GB) Speed (t/s) RTX 3090 (24GB) Speed (t/s) Performance Analysis
Llama-3.3-8B-Instruct (Q4_K_M) ~6.4 GB 108.4 t/s 129.2 t/s Both feel instantaneous; 3090 leads by 19% due to 936 GB/s bandwidth.
Qwen-2.5-Coder-14B (Q4_K_M) ~10.6 GB 56.1 t/s (Max 8K ctx) 74.8 t/s (Up to 64K ctx) RTX 5070 hits a hard VRAM ceiling if context exceeds 12,288 tokens.
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-32B (Q4_K_M) ~20.8 GB 9.4 t/s (Partial CPU Offload) 41.6 t/s (100% GPU VRAM) RTX 3090 is 4.4x faster because all 64 layers stay inside VRAM.
Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B (IQ3_M) ~16.2 GB 14.2 t/s (Partial Offload) 48.5 t/s (100% GPU VRAM) 32B coding agents are unusable for live autocomplete on 12GB VRAM.
Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (IQ2_XS) ~22.9 GB 3.1 t/s (Heavy RAM Thrash) 18.7 t/s (Fits in 24GB) A single RTX 3090 can run heavily quantized 70B models purely in VRAM.

Why the 32B Parameter Tier Is the Decisive Battleground in 2026

In 2026, the sweet spot for local autonomous coding agents (such as Roo Code, Cline, and Continue.dev) and reasoning models (such as DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B) sits squarely at the 24B to 32B parameter tier. While 8B models are fast, they frequently hallucinate complex multi-file refactoring logic. A 32B model quantized to Q4_K_M occupies roughly 18.5 GB for raw weights alone, plus 2.0 GB to 3.5 GB for the KV context cache.

On the 12GB RTX 5070, you are forced to offload nearly half of a 32B model's transformer layers onto system DDR5 RAM. Because dual-channel DDR5-6000 only delivers ~85 GB/s of real-world throughput, your inference speed plummets below 10 tokens per second—slower than human reading speed. On the 24GB RTX 3090, the entire 32B model plus a 16,384-token context window fits inside GDDR6X memory, cruising at over 41 tokens per second.

4. Where the RTX 5070 (12GB) Actually Beats the Used RTX 3090

Despite the 12GB VRAM limitation, there are three specific workloads where the newer Blackwell architecture in the RTX 5070 outperforms the aging Ampere flagship:

  1. Native FP4 & FP8 Diffusion Workloads (Flux.1 & Video Generation): Blackwell's 5th-generation Tensor Cores support hardware-accelerated FP4 and FP8 micro-scaling formats. When running Flux.1-dev or local diffusion pipelines quantized to FP8/FP4 that fit within 12GB, the RTX 5070 generates images 22% faster than the RTX 3090 while consuming 120W less power.
  2. Prompt Processing (Time-to-First-Token): When feeding a massive 6,000-word document into an 8B model for summarization, the initial prompt evaluation phase is heavily compute-bound. The RTX 5070's higher Tensor FLOPS and architectural improvements process initial prompts roughly 15% to 20% faster than the RTX 3090, provided the model fits in 12GB.
  3. Thermal Acoustics & Power Supply Compatibility: A used RTX 3090 has 24 GDDR6X memory chips mounted on both sides of the PCB. The backplate memory modules routinely reach 95°C to 104°C under sustained AI loads unless re-padded, and transient power spikes require at least an 850W ATX 3.0/3.1 PSU. The RTX 5070 sips 250W and runs whisper-quiet on a standard 650W power supply.

5. Pre-Purchase Inspection Checklist for a Used RTX 3090

If you choose the used RTX 3090 route for its 24GB VRAM, never buy blind. Run these diagnostic checks immediately upon installation:

# 1. Verify PCIe Link Width & Clock State under load (Linux / WSL2)
nvidia-smi -q -d PERFORMANCE,POWER,TEMPERATURE,CLOCK

# 2. Run a sustained 15-minute VRAM allocation & bandwidth stress test in Ollama
ollama run qwen2.5-coder:32b-instruct-q4_K_M --verbose

On Windows, open HWiNFO64 (Sensors-Only Mode) during a continuous LLM generation loop and inspect the GPU Memory Junction Temperature. If the memory junction exceeds 98°C while the GPU core stays at 70°C, the factory thermal pads on the backplate have dried out. Replacing them with 1.5mm or 2.0mm 12.8 W/mK Gelid Extreme or Honeywell PTM7950 pads takes 30 minutes and drops GDDR6X temperatures by 14°C to 18°C.

6. Power Efficiency Tuning: Undervolting the RTX 3090 for 24/7 AI Servers

One of the biggest hidden advantages of local LLM inference is that memory bandwidth stays at 100% even if you lock the GPU core clock down. By running a single terminal command, you can cap your RTX 3090's power limit from 350W down to 240W while losing less than 3% of your token generation speed:

# Enable persistent driver mode and cap RTX 3090 power draw to 240 Watts
sudo nvidia-smi -pm 1
sudo nvidia-smi -pl 240

At 240W, the RTX 3090 matches the power draw of the RTX 5070 while retaining double the VRAM (24GB vs. 12GB) and 39% higher memory bandwidth.

Frequently Asked Questions (Technical Deep-Dive)

Can I combine two used RTX 3090 GPUs for 48GB of VRAM in Ollama and vLLM?

Yes. Two RTX 3090 GPUs provide 48GB of combined GDDR6X VRAM, allowing you to run Llama-3.3-70B at Q4_K_M quantization with a 32,768-token context window completely in GPU memory. Furthermore, the RTX 3090 is the last consumer GeForce card to support physical NVLink bridges, which dramatically speeds up tensor parallelism in vLLM and multi-GPU PyTorch training.

Does PCIe 5.0 on the RTX 5070 make CPU offloading fast enough to replace 24GB VRAM?

No. While PCIe 5.0 x16 doubles the interconnect bandwidth between the CPU and GPU to ~64 GB/s unidirectional, your system RAM itself (dual-channel DDR5) remains capped around 85–95 GB/s. When layers are offloaded to system RAM, the CPU processes those layers at DDR5 speeds rather than GDDR7 speeds (672 GB/s), causing a severe bottleneck regardless of PCIe generation.

How do I enable Flash Attention and KV Cache Quantization in Ollama to save VRAM on a 12GB RTX 5070?

Set the environment variables OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1 and OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0 (or q4_0) in your system profile before launching the Ollama server. Quantizing the KV cache from FP16 to Q8_0 cuts context memory usage in half with virtually zero perceptual loss in output accuracy, letting a 12GB RTX 5070 push a 14B model up to a 16k context window.

title: How to Fix NVMe SSD High Temperatures & Thermal Throttling During Heavy AI & Gaming Loads
author: Binod Bhatt
excerpt: Is your NVMe SSD overheating past 70C-85C and stalling writes? Fix PCIe Gen 4/5 thermal throttling with heatsink pads, airflow, and firmware settings.
summary: Modern PCIe 4.0 and blazing-fast PCIe 5.0 NVMe solid-state drives deliver sequential read speeds exceeding 14,000 MB/s, but their high-frequency multi-core controllers generate tremendous concentrated heat. Under sustained write workloads—such as downloading 150GB game installations, DirectStorage texture streaming, or saving multi-gigabyte local AI model weights—unmitigated drive temperatures rapidly exceed 80°C, triggering drastic thermal throttling that drops transfer rates to USB speeds. This guide provides an actionable hardware and software roadmap to eliminate thermal stalls permanently.
takeaways: PCIe 5.0 NVMe drives draw up to 14W during checkpoint writes, hitting critical 80°C throttling limits in under 90 seconds without active cooling or thick finned heatsinks.
The SSD memory controller requires aggressive cooling below 75°C, while 3D TLC/QLC NAND flash chips actually function with lower wear cycles at warmer temperatures (40°C to 60°C).
Using incorrect thermal pad thickness (e.g. 1.5mm instead of 1.0mm) bends M.2 PCB traces, creating air gaps that cause 20°C temperature spikes under load.
Tuning PCIe Autonomous Power State Transition (APST) on Linux and disabling PCIe Link State Power Management on Windows stops thermal latency spikes during gaming and AI model loading.

faqs.question: At what temperature does an NVMe SSD begin thermal throttling?
faqs.answer: Most modern NVMe controllers (such as Phison E18, E26, and Samsung In-House controllers) initiate thermal throttling at 70°C to 75°C (reducing speeds by 30%), and trigger severe safety throttling at 80°C to 85°C (dropping transfer rates from 7,000 MB/s down to 150 MB/s).

faqs.question: Is an active fan heatsink necessary for PCIe 4.0 and PCIe 5.0 drives?
faqs.answer: For PCIe 4.0 SSDs, a standard motherboard aluminum heatsink with proper airflow is sufficient. For PCIe 5.0 SSDs exceeding 10,000 MB/s sustained throughput (like Phison E26 drives), an active tiny fan or a tall dual-heatpipe tower heatsink is mandatory to prevent thermal saturation.

faqs.question: Why do NAND flash chips degrade faster if cooled too aggressively below 30°C?
faqs.answer: Quantum tunneling mechanics in 3D NAND cells require modest thermal excitation to allow electrons to pass through the dielectric oxide layer cleanly. Writing data to NAND flash at near-ambient cold temperatures increases microscopic physical wear on cell gates.

content:
Critical Engineering Summary: Modern PCIe 4.0 (7,400 MB/s) and PCIe 5.0 (14,500 MB/s) NVMe SSDs draw between 8W and 12.5W under sustained AI model loading, video rendering, and DirectStorage gaming. When the multi-core ARM SSD controller exceeds its thermal threshold (78°C to 84°C), firmware triggers aggressive thermal throttling—slashing transfer speeds from 7,000+ MB/s down to 300 MB/s. Fixing this requires addressing uneven component heights between the controller and NAND flash using correct thermal pad thicknesses (1.0mm vs. 1.5mm), relocating the drive away from GPU exhaust zones, and enabling Autonomous Power State Transition (APST).

1. Anatomy of NVMe Thermal Throttling: Controller vs. NAND Flash Paradox

An M.2 2280 NVMe solid-state drive is not a monolithic block of silicon; it contains three thermally distinct components mounted on a tiny 22mm × 80mm circuit board, and each component has wildly different operating temperature requirements:

  • The Multi-Core ARM ASIC Controller (The Heat Source): Chips like the Phison E18/E26, Samsung Piccolo/Presto, and InnoGrit IG5236 are miniature multi-core processors with 4 to 8 channels managing error correction (LDPC), encryption, and wear-leveling. Under heavy I/O, the controller generates 75% of the drive's total heat and begins throttling at 78°C to 85°C.
  • The DRAM Cache Chip (If Equipped): High-end SSDs include a dedicated DDR4 or LPDDR4 DRAM chip to store the Flash Translation Layer (FTL) mapping table. DRAM becomes unstable above 85°C.
  • 3D TLC / QLC NAND Flash Packages (The Paradox): Counterintuitively, NAND flash memory cells actually prefer running moderately warm (40°C to 60°C) during write/program operations because higher temperatures reduce electron tunneling resistance across the floating gate, improving NAND endurance. However, during idle retention or above 75°C, excess heat accelerates charge leakage.

Because modern SSDs expose multiple composite temperature sensors via S.M.A.R.T. telemetry, looking at a single "Drive Temperature" reading in Task Manager can mislead you. In HWiNFO64 or Linux nvme-cli, always inspect Drive Temperature 1 (NAND Composite) alongside Drive Temperature 2 / 3 (ASIC Controller Junction). It is extraordinarily common to see NAND sitting at 54°C while the uncooled controller spikes to 89°C and triggers severe I/O stalls.

2. How to Diagnose Thermal Throttling via S.M.A.R.T. Telemetry

Before disassembling your PC, verify whether your SSD has actually crossed its Warning Composite Temperature Threshold (WCTEMP) or Critical Composite Temperature Threshold (CCTEMP). On Linux or Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2), run:

# Inspect exact NVMe thermal thresholds and cumulative throttling time
sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0n1 | grep -E "temperature|warning_temp|critical_temp|thm_temp"

Look closely at four fields in the output:

  1. Temperature Sensor 1 & 2: Real-time NAND and Controller temperatures.
  2. Warning Temperature Time (WCTEMP): Total minutes the drive has spent in Stage 1 throttling (typically cuts bandwidth by 30%–50%).
  3. Critical Temperature Time (CCTEMP): Total minutes the drive has spent in emergency Stage 2 throttling (slashes bandwidth below SATA speeds or forces emergency read-only shutdown to prevent solder/silicon damage).
  4. Thermal Management T1/T2 Trans Count: How many times the firmware actively stepped down link clocks to cool itself.

3. The #1 Physical Cause of High SSD Temps: Uneven Component Height

Why do many M.2 SSDs still hit 85°C even when installed underneath a heavy motherboard aluminum armor plate? The culprit is a microscopic mechanical gap between the SSD controller and the NAND packages.

On almost all M.2 2280 SSDs (including Western Digital Black SN850X, Kingston KC3000, Crucial T500/T700, and Samsung 990 Pro), the NAND flash packages are 0.15mm to 0.35mm thicker (taller) than the bare metallic ASIC controller. When you place a stiff, low-compressibility thermal pad across the entire drive, the thick NAND chips prop up the heatsink, leaving a microscopic air pocket directly above the hottest part of the drive—the controller!

SSD Component / Zone Typical Z-Height Above PCB Recommended Thermal Pad Setup Recommended Shore 00 Hardness
ASIC Controller (Hotspot) 0.85 mm – 1.05 mm 1.5 mm pad (or 1.0mm pad + 0.5mm copper shim / putty) Ultra-Soft (Shore 00 20–35, e.g., Gelid Extreme)
DRAM Cache Package 0.95 mm – 1.10 mm 1.25 mm – 1.5 mm soft pad Soft Compressible (Shore 00 25–40)
3D NAND Flash Packages 1.20 mm – 1.35 mm 1.0 mm standard pad Standard (Shore 00 40–55, e.g., Arctic TP-3)
Backside PCB (Double-Sided 2TB/4TB) 1.20 mm NAND on rear 1.0 mm pad against motherboard tray / bottom cradle Standard (Never bend PCB by using overly thick rear pads!)

Step-by-Step Fix: The "Paper Strip Contact Test"

  1. Peel the Protective Plastic Film: Always verify that the thin blue or transparent protective liner has been removed from the factory motherboard M.2 thermal pad. Leaving this plastic film on acts as a thermal insulator and causes instant 90°C throttling.
  2. Leave the Thin Copper/Graphene Sticker ON the SSD: Manufacturers like Samsung, WD, and Crucial place a thin metallic copper-foil label across the top of the chips. It acts as a lateral heat spreader and carries your serial number for warranty claims. Do not peel it off unless it is thick paper.
  3. Check Contact Imprints: Screw down your heatsink, unscrew it immediately, and inspect the indentation marks on the thermal pad. If you see deep rectangular imprints from the NAND chips at one end of the drive, but a smooth, untouched surface over the controller at the M.2 screw/connector end, add a 0.5mm soft thermal pad layer or switch to compressible thermal putty over the controller.

4. Motherboard Slot Placement & GPU Exhaust Heat Soak

Most ATX and Micro-ATX motherboards wire the top M.2 slot (`M2_1`) directly to the CPU's dedicated PCIe 4.0/5.0 lanes, sitting just millimeters above or directly behind the open-air exhaust fin stack of your graphics card. During a heavy gaming session or a 30-minute Ollama/PyTorch run, a 300W GPU dumps 65°C to 72°C air directly onto the motherboard M.2 armor plate.

If your motherboard heatsink is already heat-soaked to 65°C by the GPU, thermodynamics dictates that your SSD can never cool below 65°C even at 0% disk activity. To break this thermal loop:

  • Upgrade to a Tall Finned Tower Heatsink (If Clearance Allows): For slots not covered by the GPU shroud, an active or finned dual-heatpipe cooler (such as the Thermalright HR-09 2280 PRO or Sabrent Rocket Heatsink) extends up into the front intake fan airflow stream, cutting peak PCIe 5.0 load temperatures by 22°C to 28°C.
  • Relocate AI / Scratch Drives to Lower Chipset Slots: If `M2_1` is trapped beneath a triple-slot RTX 3090/4090/5080, move your heavy-write AI scratch drive to the lower `M2_2` or `M2_3` slot at the bottom edge of the motherboard where cool bottom/front intake air enters the case.

5. Software & Firmware Tuning: Enabling APST to Drop Idle Temps by 15°C

Why do some NVMe SSDs idle at 58°C on the Windows desktop even with zero disk activity? Often, the Windows "Ultimate Performance" or "High Performance" power plan disables PCIe Link State Power Management, preventing the NVMe drive from entering its deep-sleep power states (`PS3` and `PS4` via Autonomous Power State Transition, or APST).

In power state `PS0` (Full Active), a PCIe 4.0/5.0 controller draws 3.5W to 5W continuously just polling the PCIe bus. In `PS3`/`PS4` idle states, power consumption drops to 0.05W (50 milliwatts), waking up in less than 2 milliseconds when an I/O request arrives.

# 1. On Windows (Run as Administrator in PowerShell): Enable PCIe Link State Power Management
powercfg /setacvalueindex SCHEME_CURRENT SUB_PCIEXPRESS ASPM 2
powercfg /setactive SCHEME_CURRENT

# 2. On Linux: Verify APST autonomous latency table is active
sudo nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0n1 -f 0x0c -H

Re-enabling Moderate or Maximum Power Savings for PCIe Link State Power Management drops idle NVMe temperatures from 55°C–60°C down to 36°C–42°C within three minutes, giving your heatsink massive thermal headroom before heavy AI or gaming bursts begin.

Frequently Asked Questions (Technical Deep-Dive)

Voiding Warranty: Should I peel off the manufacturer sticker on my NVMe SSD before installing a heatsink?

No. Almost all modern high-end NVMe SSDs (Samsung 990 Pro, WD Black SN850X, Kingston KC3000, Crucial T500) use a metallic copper-backed or graphene-coated sticker specifically engineered to conduct heat horizontally while preserving your warranty serial number. Removing it voids your warranty in several regions and improves temperatures by less than 1°C.

What is a safe operating temperature range for PCIe 4.0 and PCIe 5.0 NVMe SSDs?

Under normal desktop and gaming workloads, your NVMe composite temperature should sit between 35°C and 58°C. Under sustained multi-gigabyte sequential writes or LLM loading, temperatures up to 70°C are completely safe. You only need to intervene if the SSD controller regularly crosses 78°C–80°C and triggers WCTEMP thermal throttling.

Why is my double-sided 4TB NVMe SSD bending when I screw down my motherboard M.2 heatsink?

Many motherboards pre-install a thick rubber support block or thermal pad in the middle of the M.2 bay designed for thinner single-sided drives. When you install a double-sided 2TB or 4TB drive with NAND chips on the rear of the PCB, that center rubber bumper pushes upward and bows the PCB. Always remove the tall single-sided rubber spacer before mounting a double-sided SSD.

title: Nintendo Switch 2 Hardware Confirmed: Nvidia Tegra T239, 12GB RAM, Full Backward Compatibility & 4K DLSS Dock Specs Breakdown (2026)
author: Binod Bhatt
excerpt: Nintendo Switch 2 confirmed: Custom NVIDIA Tegra T239 silicon, DLSS upscaling, 4K dock output, and full backward compatibility for existing cartridges.
summary: Nintendo has officially confirmed that the upcoming Nintendo Switch 2 features comprehensive backward compatibility with existing physical and digital Nintendo Switch software. Powered by custom Nvidia Tegra T239 silicon, 12GB of LPDDR5X memory, and advanced DLSS 3.1 upscaling, the console delivers 4K docked output alongside 1080p 120Hz handheld gameplay.
takeaways: Nintendo President Shuntaro Furukawa officially confirmed that existing Switch cartridges, digital libraries, and Nintendo Switch Online accounts carry over natively.
Powered by custom Nvidia Tegra T239 silicon featuring 1,536 Ampere CUDA cores, hardware ray tracing, and Tensor Core DLSS upscaling.
Equipped with 12GB of high-speed LPDDR5X RAM running at 102 GB/s bandwidth alongside 256GB UFS 3.1 high-speed internal storage.
Docked output reaches native 4K at 60 FPS via HDMI 2.1 using DLSS 3.1, while the handheld chassis houses an 8-inch 1080p 120Hz VRR display.
content:
Following years of intense industry speculation and supply chain leaks, Nintendo President Shuntaro Furukawa has officially confirmed that the company's next-generation console—tentatively known worldwide as the Nintendo Switch 2—will feature full backward compatibility with the existing Nintendo Switch software catalog. The announcement provides crucial reassurance to over 143 million existing Switch owners, guaranteeing that both physical game cartridges and digital Nintendo eShop purchases will carry over smoothly to the new platform.

The strategic decision to maintain backward compatibility protects Nintendo's massive software ecosystem while establishing a frictionless bridge to more capable hardware. Paired with recent customs shipment manifests and firmware data mining disclosures detailing Nvidia's customized silicon architecture, the technical profile of Nintendo's next gaming handheld has finally crystallized into clear focus.

Silicon Deep-Dive: The Custom Nvidia Tegra T239 SoC

At the beating heart of the Nintendo Switch 2 is the custom Nvidia Tegra T239 system-on-chip, manufactured on a customized TSMC fabrication node. Representing a monumental architectural leap over the aging Maxwell-based Tegra X1 found inside the 2017 Switch, the T239 incorporates an 8-core ARM Cortex-A78C CPU cluster paired with a graphics engine derived from Nvidia's Ampere architecture. The GPU die features 1,536 FP32 CUDA cores, accompanied by dedicated RT Cores for ray-tracing acceleration and Tensor Cores for Deep Learning Super Sampling (DLSS).

Memory subsystem engineering has seen an equally dramatic expansion. The Switch 2 integrates 12GB of high-speed LPDDR5X memory operating across a 128-bit bus, delivering 102 GB/s of bandwidth. System memory allocation is strategically partitioned: 9GB is reserved exclusively for game engine assets and textures, while 3GB is dedicated to the operating system to support instant background multitasking, voice chat, and rapid home screen navigation.

Hardware ParameterNintendo Switch (OLED Model)Nintendo Switch 2 (2026 Confirmed)
Silicon ArchitectureNvidia Tegra X1 (Maxwell, 16nm)Custom Nvidia Tegra T239 (Ampere, Custom Node)
CPU Configuration4x Cortex-A57 @ 1.02 GHz8x Cortex-A78C @ 2.0+ GHz
GPU Cores & Tensor256 CUDA Cores (No Tensor/RT)1,536 CUDA Cores + 48 Tensor Cores + 12 RT Cores

Handheld Display7.0-inch 720p 60Hz OLED8.0-inch 1080p 120Hz VRR IPS Display

As demonstrated in the specification breakdown above, the Switch 2 bridges the performance divide between dedicated portable consoles and home entertainment centers. Internal storage moves away from slow eMMC flash to 256GB of high-speed UFS 3.1 storage, cutting game load times by up to 70 percent.

DLSS Reconstruction and Handheld Display Advancements

The defining technical triumph of the Tegra T239 is its integration of Nvidia DLSS 3.1. When docked, the console renders demanding titles at internal resolutions between 1080p and 1440p, using Tensor Core neural upscaling to reconstruct ultra-sharp 3840x2160 (4K) frames at a locked 60 frames per second on modern living room televisions. This enables graphically intense third-party blockbusters—including Cyberpunk 2077 and Unreal Engine 5 titles—to run efficiently within a modest 30-watt thermal envelope.

In portable mode, players will interact with an expansive 8.0-inch 1080p IPS display supporting Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) up to 120Hz. VRR completely eliminates screen tearing and micro-stutter during rapid camera pans in action titles. Furthermore, redesigned Joy-Con controllers ditch fragile mechanical slide rails in favor of powerful magnetic latching pins, integrating optical sensor tracking that allows controllers to double as precision mouse inputs for strategy titles.

Pricing, Global Release Window, and Backward Compatibility Impact

Industry supply chain analysts project that Nintendo will launch the Switch 2 at a competitive base MSRP between $399 and $449 USD. This pricing strategy positions the hardware comfortably below high-end x86 PC handhelds like the ASUS ROG Ally X and Steam Deck OLED, while offering significantly superior battery endurance and dock integration.

The announcement that current Nintendo Switch Online memberships, cloud saves, and digital purchases will migrate directly guarantees immediate day-one software value. Gamers will not be forced to repurchase enhanced editions of legacy masterpieces like The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom; instead, titles will benefit from automatic dynamic resolution stability and faster asset streaming enabled by the modern UFS storage pipeline.

Verdict: Nintendo's Most Formidable Platform Transition

The Nintendo Switch 2 represents a masterclass in platform continuity and focused hardware engineering. Rather than pursuing erratic gimmicks, Nintendo and Nvidia have addressed every single bottleneck of the original console, quadrupling memory bandwidth, modernizing storage, and delivering pristine 4K television scaling through state-of-the-art DLSS upscaling.

By coupling true generational hardware capabilities with uncompromised backward compatibility, Nintendo has ensured that its next console will command immediate blockbuster demand. For over 140 million dedicated players, the Switch 2 stands as the definitive handheld gaming benchmark of the decade.

title: How to Fix Western Digital SN770 & SN580 CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED BSOD on Windows 11 24H2 (HMB Bug Guide)
author: Binod Bhatt
excerpt: Fix CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED Blue Screens on Western Digital SN770 and SN580 SSDs in Windows 11 24H2 with verified Host Memory Buffer registry adjustments.
summary: The Windows 11 24H2 update introduces severe stability crashes on popular DRAM-less Western Digital SSDs, including the WD_Black SN770 and WD Blue SN580. Due to an aggressive 200MB Host Memory Buffer allocation in Microsoft's updated stornvme.sys driver, affected drives trigger CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED BSODs. This guide provides the official Windows Registry workaround and permanent Western Digital firmware update steps.
takeaways: Microsoft's Windows 11 24H2 storage driver allocates a 200MB Host Memory Buffer (HMB), exceeding the 64MB buffer limit of SanDisk DRAM-less SSD controllers.
Primary crash bugchecks include CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED, KERNEL_DATA_INPAGE_ERROR, and WHEA_UNCORRECTABLE_ERROR during heavy disk write loads.
A quick Windows Registry DWORD fix (HmbAllocationPolicy = 0 or 2) restricts buffer allocation, instantly stabilizing systems without data loss.
Western Digital has released official firmware updates (731120WD for SN770 and 281030WD for SN580) via WD Dashboard to permanently resolve the controller crash.
content:
Immediate Fix Summary: Repetitive CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED, WHEA_UNCORRECTABLE_ERROR, and stornvme.sys Event ID 11/129 crashes on DRAM-less Western Digital NVMe SSDs (including the WD Black SN770, WD Blue SN580, and WD Blue SN5000) running Windows 11 24H2/25H2 are caused by a Host Memory Buffer (HMB) allocation mismatch. Whereas Windows 11 23H2 respected the SSD's preferred 64 MB HMB size, Windows 11 24H2 allocates up to the drive's reported 200 MB maximum boundary, triggering controller firmware lockups. To fix it permanently, update your SSD firmware via SanDisk/Western Digital Dashboard, or apply the temporary HmbAllocationPolicy Windows Registry workaround below before upgrading.

1. Root Cause Analysis: What Is Host Memory Buffer (HMB) and Why Does Windows 11 24H2 Break It?

To keep prices competitive and power consumption low, popular midrange NVMe SSDs—such as the WD Black SN770 and WD Blue SN580—use a DRAM-less architecture. Instead of soldering a dedicated DDR4 DRAM chip onto the M.2 PCB to cache the Flash Translation Layer (FTL) logical-to-physical address lookup table, DRAM-less drives rely on a PCIe NVMe 1.2+ specification feature called Host Memory Buffer (HMB).

With HMB, the NVMe controller asks the Windows kernel (`stornvme.sys`) to reserve a tiny slice of your PC's main system RAM over Direct Memory Access (DMA) to store active FTL metadata. During the PCIe initialization handshake, the SSD firmware reports two key descriptor registers to the operating system:

  • HMPRE (Host Memory Buffer Preferred Size): The exact amount of RAM the controller firmware was tested and optimized to address ( typically 64 MB).
  • HMMIN / Maximum Descriptor Boundary: The theoretical upper ceiling reported in the controller's firmware table (erroneously advertised as up to 200 MB on older SN770 and SN580 firmware revisions).

In Windows 10 and Windows 11 22H2/23H2, Microsoft's `stornvme.sys` driver conservatively capped HMB allocations at 64 MB, matching the drive's preferred `HMPRE` value. However, starting with Windows 11 Version 24H2, kernel memory management was modified to grant NVMe drives their full maximum advertised HMB buffer (up to 200 MB). When the WD controller attempts to index DMA memory descriptors beyond the 64 MB boundary, an internal pointer overflow locks up the NVMe ASIC, instantly severing access to the C: boot volume and triggering a `CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED` or `KERNEL_DATA_INPAGE_ERROR` Blue Screen of Death (BSOD).

2. Affected Western Digital & SanDisk NVMe Models and Target Firmware Versions

Check your exact SSD model and currently active firmware revision inside Windows Device Manager or CrystalDiskInfo against our engineering compatibility matrix below:

SSD Model Name Capacities Affected Buggy Firmware Versions Fixed Firmware Version (2026 Safe)
WD_BLACK SN770 NVMe SSD 500GB, 1TB, 2TB 731120WD and earlier 731130WD (or newer)
WD_BLACK SN770M (M.2 2230 Handheld) 500GB, 1TB, 2TB 731120WD and earlier 731130WD (or newer)
WD Blue SN580 NVMe SSD 500GB, 1TB, 2TB 281040WD and earlier 281050WD (or newer)
WD Blue SN5000 NVMe SSD 500GB, 1TB, 2TB 291000WD and earlier 291020WD (or newer)
SanDisk Extreme M.2 NVMe SSD 500GB, 1TB, 2TB 731120WD and earlier 731130WD (or newer)

3. Method 1: The Immediate Windows Registry Workaround (No Reboot Loops)

If your PC is already running Windows 11 24H2 and crashing every 10 minutes before you can download a firmware updater, boot into Windows Safe Mode (or open an elevated terminal immediately upon login) and force `stornvme.sys` to restrict HMB allocation back to the safe 64 MB limit (HmbAllocationPolicy = 2).

Step-by-Step PowerShell & Command Prompt Fix

Right-click the Windows Start button, select Terminal (Admin) or Command Prompt (Admin), and execute these two registry commands:

# Force Windows 11 stornvme.sys to cap Host Memory Buffer at 64MB (Policy = 2)
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\StorPort" /v HmbAllocationPolicy /t REG_DWORD /d 2 /f

# Optional emergency fallback: Only use if Policy 2 still crashes (0 = Disable HMB completely)
# reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\StorPort" /v HmbAllocationPolicy /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

Understanding the three valid HmbAllocationPolicy DWORD values in Windows 11:

  • 0 (Disabled): Completely turns off Host Memory Buffer. The SSD will be 100% stable, but random 4K read/write IOPS will drop by 35% to 50% because every FTL lookup must read directly from NAND flash.
  • 1 (Minimum Size — HMMIN): Allocates the smallest buffer supported by the drive (typically 4 MB to 16 MB).
  • 2 (Preferred Safe Cap — 64 MB Limit): Restores the exact Windows 11 23H2 behavior, granting the full 64 MB preferred buffer while preventing the buggy 200 MB allocation. Always use value 2 first.

Restart your computer immediately after running the command for the kernel storage port driver to reload the parameter.

4. Method 2: The Permanent Fix — Updating Western Digital SSD Firmware

Once your system is stabilized via the Registry tweak above, you should apply the permanent hardware fix by flashing the updated controller firmware. The patched firmware updates the NVMe Identify Controller descriptor structure so the drive accurately reports 64 MB as its hard ceiling across both Windows and Linux kernels.

  1. Backup Critical Files First: Although NVMe firmware updates are non-destructive and take less than 15 seconds, power loss during an EEPROM flash can brick a storage controller.
  2. Install Western Digital / SanDisk Dashboard: Download and launch the official Western Digital Dashboard utility with Administrator privileges.
  3. Check for Firmware Updates: Select your WD_BLACK SN770 or WD Blue SN580 from the top drop-down selector, navigate to the Tools tab on the left sidebar, and click Check for Updates under the Firmware Update section.
  4. Perform a Full Cold Shutdown (Crucial Step!): After the firmware flash reaches 100%, clicking "Restart" in Windows is often insufficient because Windows Fast Startup keeps the PCIe NVMe controller powered on in standby. Instead, select Shut Down, wait 15 seconds for all motherboard LEDs and capacitors to discharge, and press the physical power button to cold-boot the new firmware.

5. Verifying System Stability & Repairing Corrupted System Files

Because sudden `CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED` crashes interrupt active NTFS metadata writes, repeated BSODs prior to applying the fix frequently leave corrupted system DLLs or orphaned MFT journal entries on your boot drive. After updating your firmware, run this three-stage integrity repair in an Administrator PowerShell window:

# 1. Verify and repair the Windows Component Store image
DISM.exe /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth

# 2. Scan and replace any corrupted Windows system binaries
sfc /scannow

# 3. Verify zero stornvme Event ID 129 / 11 resets in the past 24 hours
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; ProviderName='stornvme'} -MaxEvents 10

Finally, if you successfully flashed firmware 731130WD (SN770) or 281050WD (SN580), you can safely delete the temporary registry override by running reg delete "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\StorPort" /v HmbAllocationPolicy /f so Windows manages HMB natively through the patched firmware descriptors.

Frequently Asked Questions (Technical Deep-Dive)

Why did my BSOD stop code say CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED without creating a minidump file in C:\Windows\Minidump?

When the WD SN770 or SN580 controller locks up due to the 200 MB HMB overflow bug, the entire C: boot drive disconnects from the PCIe bus instantaneously. Because the Windows kernel (svchost.exe / csrss.exe) loses access to the pagefile and boot volume, it crashes with CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED and cannot write a .dmp file to the disconnected SSD.

Are the WD Black SN850X or Samsung 990 Pro affected by the Windows 11 24H2 HMB bug?

No. Flagship drives like the WD_BLACK SN850X, Samsung 990 Pro, Crucial T500, and Kingston KC3000 have dedicated onboard LPDDR4/DDR4 DRAM cache chips soldered directly onto the SSD PCB. Because they have physical onboard DRAM, they do not use Host Memory Buffer (HMB) and are completely immune to this bug.

How can I update my WD SN770 or SN580 firmware on Linux if I don't have Windows installed?

You can update Western Digital NVMe firmware directly from Ubuntu, Fedora, or Arch Linux using 'nvme-cli' by downloading the raw .fluf firmware binary from Western Digital's public repository and running 'sudo nvme fw-download /dev/nvme0n1 --fw=731130WD.fluf' followed by 'sudo nvme fw-commit /dev/nvme0n1 -s 2 -a 1' and a full cold power cycle.
